# DISCUSSION

  The rescue and compilation of this dataset presented several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results and using the data for future research. The monitoring program was conducted over an extended period, during which different field crews were involved in data collection, and sampling often took place in remote areas resulting in lakes being less surveyed than others. These circumstances may have contributed to inconsistencies in data collection and recording. Furthermore, the sampling methodology was developed and modified throughout the implementation of the program, potentially introducing temporal differences in sampling procedures and limiting direct comparisons among years.

  Additional challenges were encountered during data rescue and standardization. Scale books and scale book identification numbers were not standardized, making it difficult to determine the meaning of some codes and their correspondence to specific sampling events or records. Fish length and weight measurements were also recorded using different units (cm/mm and g/mg, respectively), requiring careful examination and standardization to ensure data accuracy. Despite these efforts, some values may remain unconverted or incorrectly recorded. Missing data represent another important limitation, including gaps within years for which rescued data were available. This issue was particularly evident in the trawl dataset, for which no data could be recovered yet for the period from 2000 to 2007. Consequently, data availability and completeness should be evaluated before conducting analyses, particularly those requiring consistent temporal coverage or comparisons among sampling periods.

  Despite these limitations, the program represents one of the most extensive and long-standing lake monitoring initiatives in the region, resulting in a comprehensive dataset with considerable value for fisheries and ecological research. The Acoustic-Trawl Survey (ATS) dataset encompasses multiple information about fish populations and their environment, including species composition, morphological characteristics (length and weight), sampling depth, geographical distribution, and abundance. Together, these data provide opportunities to investigate changes in fish communities over time and space (biogeographic estimations), modelling species distribution, examine species-specific habitat associations and biological requirements, and assess patterns of abundance and distribution.

  The long-term and multidimensional nature of this dataset provides a valuable foundation for future research, including ecological analyses, fisheries stock assessments, and investigations of lake productivity. Although data inconsistencies and gaps must be acknowledged, documenting these limitations and applying appropriate quality-control procedures will help maximize the scientific value of the rescued data. Overall, preserving and making this legacy dataset accessible represents an important contribution to future research, particularly in the context of understanding long-term changes in lake ecosystems and fish populations.
